blocks.title: How to use these questions
bullets: Read the lesson for that task first. These questions are for **step five** — writing independently — not for step one.
Write by hand. You will write the examination by hand.
Set a timer. Practising without time pressure prepares you for an examination that has it.
Correct your own work afterwards with the checklist from the lesson. This matters more than doing another question.

hero.text: Answers to take apart, not to memorise. Under every one is a set of notes explaining what makes it work.

blocks.title: Read this before you read the answers
bullets: These are **teaching materials written by RCF English**. They are not official answers, and they are not the only acceptable answers.
**Do not memorise them.** An answer copied from a website into an examination script is easy for an examiner to spot and does not fit the question you were actually asked.
Use them the way a carpenter uses a finished chair: to see how the joints are made.
Read the notes under each answer. The notes are the lesson; the answer is only the example.

blocks.heading: How to study a model answer
numbered: Read the question, and give yourself two minutes to plan an answer of your own before you look at the model.
Read the model once for what it says.
Read it again and mark the parts: where does it open, where is the main information, where does it close?
Read the notes and check whether you had spotted each point yourself.
Cover the model and write your own answer to the same question.
Compare, and note the **one** thing you would change. One improvement made is worth ten noticed.

items.label: Notice
items.prompt: As the secretary of the Environmental Club, write a notice inviting students to take part in a tree-planting programme.
sample: **ST JOHN'S COLLEGE — ENVIRONMENTAL CLUB**
**NOTICE**
5 September
**TREE-PLANTING PROGRAMME**
The Environmental Club will conduct a tree-planting programme in the school grounds on Saturday, 20 September, from 8 a.m. to 11 a.m.
Students of all grades may take part. Saplings and tools will be provided by the club. Participants are requested to come in games clothes and to bring a bottle of water.
Those who wish to join should give their names to the undersigned before Wednesday, 17 September.
N. Dissanayake
Secretary, Environmental Club
notes: All the essential parts are present: organisation, NOTICE, date, heading, body, name and position.
The first line of the body answers what, when and where in a single sentence.
The second paragraph answers who may come and what they must bring — the practical questions a reader will have.
The third paragraph gives the action required and a deadline with a day and a date.
There is no greeting and no closing phrase, because a notice has neither.
The whole thing is under eighty words. A notice should be short.

items.label: Formal email
items.prompt: Write an email to the manager of a bookshop enquiring about books for O/L English revision, and asking about prices and delivery to your town.
sample: **Subject:** Enquiry about O/L English revision books
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am a Grade 11 student preparing for the G.C.E. Ordinary Level examination, and I am writing to enquire about revision books for English.

I should like to know which titles you have for O/L English grammar and writing practice, and whether you also stock books of past papers with answers. If you could send me the titles and the current prices, I should be grateful.

I live in Weliketiya, which is some distance from your shop. Could you also let me know whether you deliver books to this area, what the delivery charge would be, and how long delivery normally takes?
Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to your reply.
Yours faithfully,
A. Bandara
notes: The subject line states the purpose in six words.
*Dear Sir or Madam* is used because the reader's name is unknown, so the closing is *Yours faithfully*.
The first sentence establishes who the writer is and why they are writing. The reader now knows how to answer.
The questions are grouped by subject: books and prices in one paragraph, delivery in the next. Grouping questions makes them easy to answer, and an easy question gets a quicker reply.
Each question is specific. *Please send details* would have been much weaker.
The tone is polite and formal throughout, with full forms rather than short forms.

items.label: Paragraph
items.prompt: Write a paragraph about a person who has influenced you.
sample: The person who has influenced me most is my grandmother, although she never went beyond Grade 8 at school. She could not help me with my homework, but she taught me something I have found more useful: how to keep going when a thing is difficult. When I failed my first term test in mathematics and refused to open the book again, she did not scold me and she did not comfort me. She simply sat beside me every evening for a month with her own knitting, saying nothing, until sitting at that table became ordinary again. My marks improved slowly, but what changed permanently was my belief that a bad result is a starting point rather than a verdict. I have used that lesson far more often than anything I learnt in a classroom.
notes: The topic sentence names the person and hints at something unexpected — that she was uneducated — which makes the reader want the next sentence.
The paragraph has **one** idea: what this person taught the writer. It does not wander into her cooking, her health or her other grandchildren.
The detail is concrete and specific: a failed mathematics test, a month of evenings, her knitting. Concrete detail is what separates a strong paragraph from a general one.
The writing shows rather than tells. It never says *she was patient*; it describes her sitting there for a month, which is more convincing.
The concluding sentence lifts the paragraph from an anecdote to a point, and does not merely repeat the opening.

items.label: Argumentative essay
items.prompt: Should students be given homework every day? Give your opinion.
sample: Almost every school day ends with the same instruction, and almost every student greets it with the same sigh. Homework is so ordinary a part of school life that it is rarely questioned at all. Yet the question is worth asking, because the amount of homework a student is given each day has a direct effect on both their learning and their health. In my view homework is valuable, but daily homework in every subject is not.

The argument for homework is a strong one. A lesson heard once is easily lost, and work done at home is often the only time a student practises alone, without a teacher standing by. In language learning this is particularly true: nobody has ever learnt to write English by watching someone else write it. Homework also builds the habit of working without supervision, which every student will need after school, whatever they go on to do.

The difficulty is not homework itself but its quantity. A student taking nine subjects, each teacher assigning work "for tomorrow", may face four hours of it after a seven-hour school day and a long journey home. At that point the purpose is defeated. Work done at eleven o'clock at night by an exhausted student teaches nothing; it is copied, rushed, or left undone, and the student learns only to feel guilty. Sleep, exercise and family time are not luxuries taken away from study — they are the conditions that make study possible.

There is also a fairness question that is easily forgotten. Not every home is a place where homework can be done. A student with electricity, a table and a quiet room is not competing on equal terms with one who shares a single room with five people, or who must help in a shop until closing time. Homework set carelessly widens a gap that school is supposed to narrow.

My conclusion is therefore not that homework should be abolished, but that it should be limited and coordinated. A reasonable amount, set by agreement between teachers rather than by each teacher separately, and designed to be finished in an hour, would give students the benefit of independent practice without the exhaustion and the unfairness. Homework should be a tool, not a habit; and like every tool, it works best when it is used deliberately.
notes: The introduction narrows from a general observation to the specific question, and ends with a clear position. The position is genuinely arguable rather than *there are both advantages and disadvantages*.
Each body paragraph has one job: paragraph two argues for homework, paragraph three against too much of it, paragraph four raises fairness.
The essay **answers the opposing view rather than ignoring it**. This is what an argumentative essay is judged on.
Concrete detail again does the work: nine subjects, four hours, eleven o'clock, a shared room. Compare how much weaker *too much homework is bad for students* would be.
The conclusion does not repeat the introduction. It moves to a practical proposal and closes with a short, memorable sentence.
The linking is varied — *The argument for*, *The difficulty is*, *There is also*, *My conclusion is therefore* — rather than *Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly*.

pages.title: Examination Techniques
pages.description: Practical examination technique for O/L English: reading the question properly, dividing your time, planning briefly, and using the last ten minutes well.
pages.keywords: exam technique, O/L English, time management, reading the question, checking answers

hero.text: Every year, students lose more marks to poor technique than to poor English. Technique can be fixed in a week.

blocks.heading: The four failures that cost most marks
text: Almost every avoidable loss of marks in an English paper falls into one of these four.
numbered: **Not answering the question that was asked.** The student answers a question they prepared for, or answers half of a two-part question.
**Running out of time.** A long, careful answer to question two, and nothing at all for question four.
**Ignoring the form.** Writing a notice as a letter, or an email as an essay. The English may be excellent; the marks are not.
**Not checking.** Ten minutes of checking recovers marks that took an hour to earn.

items.title: Read it twice
text: Once quickly, once with a pen in your hand. The second reading is where you notice the word you missed.

items.title: Underline the instruction words
text: *Describe*, *explain*, *compare*, *give two reasons*, *in your own words*, *in about 100 words*, *write a letter to*. Each of these changes what a correct answer looks like.

items.title: Count the parts
text: *Explain what happened and say how you felt* is two tasks. Write a small **(2)** in the margin so you cannot forget the second one.

items.title: Look at the marks
text: A one-mark question wants a few words. A five-mark question wants five points, or one point developed five ways. The marks tell you the length.

items.title: Note the form and the reader
text: Before writing, say to yourself: *This is a formal letter to a stranger.* That single sentence prevents the most expensive mistakes.

blocks.heading: Dividing your time
text: Do this in the first two minutes, before you write anything.

Then obey the clock. If your time for a question is finished, stop and move on, even mid-sentence if necessary; you can return at the end. An unattempted question scores nothing, and nothing is the lowest score there is.
numbered: Note the total working time and subtract ten minutes for checking.
Divide the remainder between the questions in proportion to their marks.
Write the **finishing time** for each question in the margin of your answer sheet — not the number of minutes, the actual clock time. Under pressure, arithmetic is the first thing to go.

blocks.heading: In the hall
do: Number your answers exactly as the paper numbers its questions.
Leave a line between answers so the examiner can see where one ends.
Cross out rough work with a single line — never scribble over it.
Write legibly, especially in the last fifteen minutes.
Keep going when you are stuck on one item; come back to it.
dont: Write a long introduction before answering.
Answer more questions than required, hoping for the best marks to be counted.
Rewrite an answer neatly — you do not have time, and marks are for content and accuracy.
Spend the last ten minutes writing more instead of checking.
Panic over one difficult item; it is worth a small number of marks.

blocks.heading: The last ten minutes
text: Do not use them to write more. Use them in this order — the items at the top recover the most marks for the least effort.
items: Have I **attempted every question** and every part of every question?
Are my **answer numbers** correct and clear?
In each piece of writing, is the **form** the one that was asked for?
Check the **verbs**: read each sentence looking only at the verb, and at whether it agrees with its subject.
Check **a, an, the** — the errors most students make most often.
Check **capital letters** at the start of sentences, and on names, days, months and places.
Check **full stops** — especially that two sentences have not been joined with a comma.
Check the **spellings you know you get wrong**. Everyone has five or six; learn yours.
Is my **name and index number** on the paper?

blocks.heading: In the week before
bullets: **Do one complete paper under full examination conditions.** Not a section — a whole paper, timed, by hand, in one sitting. This is the single most useful thing you can do, and most students never do it.
**Rewrite one answer you did badly.** Rewriting one weak answer teaches more than writing three new ones.
**Re-read your own corrected work**, not new material. Your own mistakes are the most efficient thing you can revise.
**Sleep.** A tired brain reads questions carelessly, and careless reading is the largest single cause of lost marks.

pages.title: Common Student Mistakes
pages.description: The English errors that cost O/L students the most marks, each shown wrong and right, with the reason behind the correction and practice to fix them.
pages.keywords: common mistakes English, common errors, O/L English, grammar errors, correction

hero.text: The same errors appear year after year. Fix ten of them and your writing improves more than it would from a month of new material.

blocks.title: How to use this page
text: Do not read it all at once. Take one table, find two examples of that error in your own recent written work, and correct them. Repeat with the next table tomorrow.
An error you have found in your own writing is fixed; an error you have only read about is not.

blocks.heading: Verbs and tenses
rows: With he, she or it, the negative is *doesn't*.
Third person singular takes *-s* in the simple present.
*Since* with a continuing situation needs the present perfect.
Do not use the present perfect with a finished time.
After *did*, the main verb returns to its base form.
*Have* meaning possession is not used in the continuous.
State verbs are not used in the continuous.
The work does not complete itself; the passive is needed.

blocks.heading: Nouns, articles and agreement
rows: *Information* is uncountable and has no plural.
*Furniture* is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
*Every* is followed by a singular noun.
One of my friend is a doctor.
One of my **friends** is a doctor.
*One of* is followed by a plural noun.
A singular countable noun needs an article.
*Hour* begins with a vowel sound, so *an* is used.
The box of books are heavy.
The verb agrees with *box*, not with *books*.
Each of the boys have a bag.
Each of the boys **has** a bag.

blocks.heading: Prepositions and word partnerships
rows: *Discuss* takes a direct object with no preposition.
*Marry* takes a direct object. *Married to* is used with *be*.
*Listen* is followed by *to* when there is an object.
*Repeat* already means to do it again.
I look forward to hear from you.
I look forward to **hearing** from you.
Here *to* is a preposition, so the *-ing* form follows.

blocks.heading: Sentence structure
rows: He asked me where do I live.
Reported questions use normal statement order.
Although it rained, but we went.
Because he was ill. He did not come.
**Because he was ill, he did not come.**
A *because* clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.
I like reading, I read every day.
I like reading**;** I read every day.
Two sentences cannot be joined with only a comma.
If it will rain, we will stay.
*Will* does not go in the if-clause.
He is more taller than me.
Do not use *more* with an *-er* comparative.
It is the most best answer.
Being a rainy day, we stayed home.
**As it was a rainy day**, we stayed home.
The original leaves the participle without a proper subject.

blocks.heading: Words that are confused
rows: He gave me a good advise.
*Advice* is the noun; *advise* is the verb.
*Lose* is the verb; *loose* means not tight.
*Principal* is the head; *principle* is a rule or belief.
*Everyday* as one word is an adjective, as in *everyday clothes*.
*Cousin brother* is not used in standard English.
*Revert* means to return to a previous state, not to reply.

blocks.heading: Practise correcting errors
intro: Each sentence contains one mistake. Rewrite the whole sentence correctly.

blocks.heading: Build your own error list
text: Everyone has a personal set of about six errors that they make repeatedly. They are not the same for everyone, and a general list can never replace your own.

Take the last three pieces of written work you had corrected. Write down every error, and count how often each kind appears. The two or three that appear most often are your list. Put it inside the cover of your exercise book and check every piece of writing against it before you hand it in.
Students who do this usually eliminate their commonest error within a month.

hero.text: Practice that marks itself and explains every answer. No login, nothing recorded, and you can start any activity again.

blocks.title: A revision method that works
bullets: **Read the lesson first**, then do the activity. Practice after an explanation teaches far more than practice instead of one.
**Answer before you look.** Getting it wrong and then reading why is one of the most effective ways to learn.
**Read every explanation**, including for the answers you got right — you may have been right for the wrong reason.
**Repeat after a few days.** Coming back to the same activity later is what moves knowledge into permanent memory.
